segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan Cohort.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day we put in at Sidon, and Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends and be cared for.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Putting out to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and after sailing across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came down to Myra in Lycia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us aboard it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For a good many days we sailed slowly and arrived off Cnidus with difficulty. Since the wind would not let us go on, we sailed under the lee of Crete, off Salmone,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since a good deal of time had passed and the voyage was by now dangerous, because even the Fast had already gone by, Paul gave his advice,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Men, I can see that the voyage is going to bring damage and heavy loss, not only of the cargo and the ship but also of our lives.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and the shipowner rather than by what Paul said.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since the harbor was unsuitable for wintering in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, in the hope of somehow reaching Phoenix and wintering there—a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had achieved their purpose; they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close inshore.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But before long a wind of hurricane force, called the Northeaster, swept down from the island.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The ship was caught up and could not face into the wind, so we gave way and were carried along.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to get control of the ship’s boat.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After hoisting it aboard, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear and so were carried along.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As we were being violently battered by the storm, the next day they began to jettison the cargo,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When neither sun nor stars had appeared for many days and no small storm kept pressing on us, all hope of our being saved was finally being taken away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up among them and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Men, you should have listened to me and not put out to sea from Crete, and spared yourselves this damage and loss.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now I advise you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood by me

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and said,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar; and look, God has granted you all those who are sailing with you.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So take heart, men, for I trust God that it will be just as I have been told.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But we must run aground on some island.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the fourteenth night came, as we were drifting across the Sea of Adria, about midnight the sailors began to suspect that they were nearing land.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They took a sounding and found twenty fathoms; a little farther on they took another sounding and found fifteen fathoms.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Fearing that we might run aground somewhere on the rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the sailors tried to escape from the ship and lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they were going to lay out anchors from the bow,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the boat and let it fall away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As day was about to break, Paul urged everyone to take some food, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Today is the fourteenth day that you have been waiting in suspense and going without food, taking nothing.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So I urge you to take some food; this is for your survival, for not a hair from the head of any of you will be lost.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After saying this, he took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it, and began to eat.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they all took heart, and they too took some food.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In all we were two hundred seventy-six people on the ship.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had eaten their fill, they began lightening the ship by throwing the grain into the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When day came, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, and they planned to run the ship ashore on it if they could.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time untying the ropes that held the steering oars. Then they hoisted the foresail to the wind and made for the beach.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they came upon a spot where two seas met and ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck fast and remained immovable, while the stern was being broken up by the violence.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them could swim away and escape.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the centurion, wanting to bring Paul safely through, kept them from carrying out their intention. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for land,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the rest to follow, some on planks and others on pieces from the ship. And so it came about that all were brought safely through to land.

notes.note: A cohort was a Roman army unit of several hundred men. “Augustan” was an honorary title given to some auxiliary units, and inscriptions attest a cohort with this title stationed in Syria in the first century. Whether that is the unit meant here cannot be proved.

“The Fast” is the Day of Atonement, which falls in late September or early October. Ancient sailors regarded the open Mediterranean as dangerous from about mid-September and closed to shipping from about mid-November until spring, so the voyage was already running into the risky season.

notes.traditional: lieth toward the south west and north west
notes.note: The Greek says the harbor looks “along” the southwest wind and the northwest wind. This may mean it faces the quarters those winds blow from (southwest and northwest), or the directions toward which they blow (northeast and southeast). The choice affects which bay on the south coast of Crete is meant, and the identification remains disputed.

The earliest manuscripts give the wind’s name as Eurakylon, a sailors’ compound of the Greek word for the east wind and the Latin word for the north wind, hence an east-northeast gale. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “Euroclydon”. Most modern versions translate the name as here.

The Syrtis was the name for the gulfs off the coast of Libya, whose shallows and shifting sandbanks were notorious among ancient sailors. A ship driven southwest from Crete by a northeast gale would be heading toward them.

The Greek word is a general term for equipment. The crew may have lowered the mainsail and its yard to reduce the ship’s speed, or let down a sea anchor to drag behind and slow the drift. The translation keeps the general word because the Greek does not specify.

In the first century this name covered not only the modern Adriatic but the central Mediterranean between Greece and Crete on one side and Italy and Sicily on the other. A ship drifting west from Crete toward Malta was therefore in “Adria”.

notes.phrase: he took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it
notes.note: The sequence of taking bread, giving thanks and breaking it echoes Luke’s accounts of Jesus feeding the crowds and of the Last Supper. Most interpreters understand this as the ordinary Jewish thanksgiving before a meal, since most of those present were not believers, though Luke probably intends the echo. Some see a celebration of the Lord’s Supper.

The Greek word, often rendered “soul”, is used here in the Septuagint manner to count individuals, as in the older English “two hundred souls on board”. “People” gives the plain sense; in verses 10 and 22 the same word is rendered “life”.

notes.phrase: a spot where two seas met
notes.traditional: a place where two seas met
notes.note: The rare Greek adjective means literally “of two seas”. It may describe a sandbank or reef with water on both sides, which is why many modern versions have “sandbar” or “reef”, or a channel or point of land where two bodies of water meet. The translation keeps the literal sense because the exact feature is uncertain.

notes.traditional: with the violence of the waves
notes.note: Many manuscripts read “the violence of the waves”. The earliest witnesses lack “of the waves”, and the Greek text translated here follows them; the pounding of the surf is in any case what is meant.
Roman soldiers were held personally answerable for prisoners in their charge and could pay with their own lives if one escaped. Acts 12:19 and 16:27 show the same rule at work.

notes.traditional: on broken pieces of the ship
notes.note: The Greek says literally “on some of the ones from the ship”, and the form could refer to things or to people. Most translators understand pieces of wreckage; a minority take it to mean that some who could not swim were carried by members of the crew.

candidates.reason: The verb and its noun σωτηρία (rendered “survival” in v. 34) range from physical rescue to final salvation across the New Testament, and versions vary between “save”, “rescue”, “heal” and “make well” in ways that hide the shared word.
The term recurs in the passion narratives and Acts, and versions vary between “band”, “cohort”, “regiment”, “battalion” and “detachment”.
Very frequent across Acts and the letters with senses of urge, appeal, encourage and comfort; the lines between them need one policy.
Versions divide between “Caesar” and “the emperor” throughout the Gospels and Acts, and the choice should be uniform.
The word means the Roman province in western Asia Minor, not the continent; a single decision is needed on “Asia” versus “the province of Asia” across Acts, the letters and Revelation.

warnings: Verse 1: παραδίδωμι is not rendered with a register form (hand over; hand on; hand down; give up; give over; entrust; risk; be ripe) and has no register-exception note.

Verse 10: ψυχή is not rendered with a register form (life; soul; person / people / everyone / human being; living being / living creature; mind; wholeheartedly; keep in suspense) and has no register-exception note.
